Getting Help and Troubleshooting

Source: vignettes/getting-help.Rmd
getting-help.Rmd

Welcome to the spconform help and troubleshooting guide. Whether you are fitting spatial conformal prediction intervals for the first time, diagnosing empirical coverage, or interfacing custom machine learning models, this guide provides answers to common questions, error diagnoses, model integration recipes, and guidelines for reporting issues.

1. Quick Support Matrix

Need Recommended Channel Details
Bug Reports & Crashes GitHub Issues Provide a minimal reproducible example (reprex) and sessionInfo().
Model Advice & Theory GitHub Issues (Question) Questions on spatial exchangeability, choice of kernel, or sample size.
Feature Requests GitHub Issues (Enhancement) Propose new diagnostic metrics, weight kernels, or interface integrations.
Academic Inquiries Direct Email Reach maintainer Ahmed Sattar Jabbar at ahmed.state.me@gmail.com.

2. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q1: My empirical coverage is slightly below 1−α1 - \alpha (e.g. 88.5% instead of 90%). Is my model invalid?

Not necessarily. Conformal prediction guarantees valid marginal coverage in expectation: P(Yn+1∈Ĉ(Sn+1))≥1−αP\left(Y_{n+1} \in \widehat{C}(S_{n+1})\right) \ge 1 - \alpha For any finite test evaluation set of size mm, the observed empirical coverage follows a Binomial distribution Binom(m,1−α)\text{Binom}(m, 1 - \alpha) with standard error: SE=α(1−α)m\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha(1 - \alpha)}{m}} For example, with m=100m = 100 and nominal coverage 90%90\% (α=0.10\alpha = 0.10), the standard error is 0.1×0.9/100=0.03\sqrt{0.1 \times 0.9 / 100} = 0.03 (3%3\%). An observed coverage between 84%84\% and 96%96\% falls well within normal 95%95\% binomial sampling variation. You can compute the exact binomial confidence interval via:

report <- coverage_report(out, y_test)
binom.test(round(report$coverage * length(y_test)), length(y_test), p = 1 - out$alpha)

Q2: Should I use scp_geostatistical() or scp_areal()?

  • Use scp_geostatistical() when observations have continuous coordinates (x,y)(x, y) or (lon,lat)(\text{lon}, \text{lat}), such as weather stations, air quality sensors, or soil core samples.
  • Use scp_areal() when data are aggregated over discrete spatial units (counties, municipalities, census tracts, or lattice grid cells) where relationships are defined by an adjacency matrix WW.

Q3: How does spatial bandwidth affect interval widths?

  • In scp_geostatistical(), weights decay as wi=exp⁡(−∥s0−si∥2/(2h2))w_i = \exp(-\|s_0 - s_i\|^2 / (2h^2)).
    • A smaller hh restricts calibration to immediately proximate neighbors, producing localized intervals that adapt to local heteroscedasticity, but may be noisy if local data are sparse.
    • A larger hh borrows strength from more calibration points, yielding smoother, more stable intervals that approach standard split conformal prediction.
    • The default (bandwidth = NULL) employs the median pairwise distance heuristic, which provides a robust balance for isotropic spatial domains.

Q4: Does spconform support spatio-temporal data?

Yes. Supply t_train and t0 alongside coordinates in scp_geostatistical():

out <- scp_geostatistical(
  s_train = s_train, y_train = y_train, s0 = s_test,
  pred_fun = my_st_predictor,
  t_train = t_train, t0 = t_test,
  temporal_bandwidth = 7,  # e.g. 7 days
  alpha = 0.1
)

3. Interpreting the Diagnostic Suite (diagnose())

The diagnose() function conducts five audits on spatial prediction intervals:

diag <- diagnose(out, y_true = y_test, s_test = s_test, plot = TRUE)
print(diag)

1. Marginal Coverage & Interval Width

  • coverage: Fraction of true values falling within [L(s0),U(s0)][L(s_0), U(s_0)]. Should be ≥1−α\ge 1 - \alpha.
  • mean_width vs median_width: If the mean width is substantially larger than the median, spatial outliers or high-uncertainty boundary clusters are inflating interval widths.

2. Winkler Interval Score (WIS)

A strictly proper scoring rule balancing interval sharpness and miscoverage penalties: WISα(l,u,y)=(u−l)+2α(l−y)𝟏(y<l)+2α(y−u)𝟏(y>u)\text{WIS}_\alpha(l, u, y) = (u - l) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(l - y)\mathbf{1}(y < l) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y - u)\mathbf{1}(y > u) Lower scores indicate superior predictive performance (narrower intervals with minimal violations).

3. Spatial Quadrant Stratification

Partitions the 2D spatial bounding box into n×nn \times n quadrants (default 4×4=164 \times 4 = 16). * Inspect whether any specific quadrant suffers severe localized under-coverage (e.g. coverage <75%< 75\%). * Local deficits often highlight unobserved spatial covariates or sharp topographical transitions.

4. Convex Hull Boundary Proximity

Examines whether intervals near the edge of the spatial domain experience degraded coverage due to spatial extrapolation. diagnose() partitions test points into Interior vs. Boundary units.

5. Spatial Autocorrelation (Moran’s II)

Computes Moran’s II on absolute conformal residuals: * I≈0I \approx 0 (p>0.05p > 0.05): Nonconformity scores are spatially independent; local exchangeability holds well. * I>0I > 0 (p<0.05p < 0.05): Prediction errors cluster spatially, indicating unmodeled spatial autocorrelation in the underlying point predictor.

4. Model Integration Recipes (pred_fun)

spconform is strictly model-agnostic. The pred_fun must have the signature: function(s_train, y_train, s_new) and return a plain 1D numeric vector of length nrow(s_new).

Recipe 1: Random Forest (ranger) 

library(ranger)

pred_rf <- function(s_train, y_train, s_new) {
  df_tr <- data.frame(x = s_train[, 1], y = s_train[, 2], target = y_train)
  df_te <- data.frame(x = s_new[, 1],   y = s_new[, 2])
  
  fit <- ranger(target ~ x + y, data = df_tr, num.trees = 100)
  predict(fit, data = df_te)$predictions
}

Recipe 2: Generalized Additive Model (mgcv::gam) 

library(mgcv)

pred_gam <- function(s_train, y_train, s_new) {
  df_tr <- data.frame(x = s_train[, 1], y = s_train[, 2], target = y_train)
  df_te <- data.frame(x = s_new[, 1],   y = s_new[, 2])
  
  fit <- gam(target ~ s(x, y, k = 20), data = df_tr)
  as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = df_te))
}

Recipe 3: Ordinary Spatial Kriging (gstat) 

library(sp)
library(gstat)

pred_kriging <- function(s_train, y_train, s_new) {
  sp_tr <- SpatialPointsDataFrame(coords = s_train, data = data.frame(y = y_train))
  sp_te <- SpatialPoints(coords = s_new)
  
  vgm_mod <- fit.variogram(variogram(y ~ 1, sp_tr), vgm("Exp"))
  krig_out <- krige(y ~ 1, sp_tr, sp_te, model = vgm_mod, debug.level = 0)
  krig_out$var1.pred
}

5. Troubleshooting Common Errors

Error: s_train and s0 must have the same number of coordinate columns

  • Cause: The number of columns in the training coordinate matrix does not match the query points (e.g. 2D training coordinates vs 3D spatio-temporal queries).
  • Fix: Verify dimensions with ncol(s_train) == ncol(s0).

Error: s_train and y_train must have the same number of observations

  • Cause: Coordinate rows do not align with response vector length, or missing values were filtered from one object but not the other.

  • Fix: Synchronize rows prior to calling spconform:

    valid_idx <- complete.cases(s_train, y_train)
s_train <- s_train[valid_idx, , drop = FALSE]
y_train <- y_train[valid_idx]

Warning: Effective neighbourhood weight vanishingly small; falling back to unweighted quantile

  • Cause: In scp_areal(), an areal target unit has no graph neighbors in the training set (an isolated island or disconnected graph component).
  • Fix: Check adjacency matrix connectivity using rowSums(adjacency). Ensure graph adjacency accurately connects all target units.

6. Submitting a Minimal Reproducible Example (reprex)

If you encounter unexpected behavior, please create a self-contained reproducible example:

library(spconform)

# 1. Synthetic reproducible dataset
set.seed(42)
n_tr <- 80
n_te <- 20
s_train <- matrix(runif(n_tr * 2), ncol = 2)
y_train <- sin(3 * s_train[, 1]) + rnorm(n_tr, sd = 0.2)

s_test  <- matrix(runif(n_te * 2), ncol = 2)
y_test  <- sin(3 * s_test[, 1])  + rnorm(n_te, sd = 0.2)

# 2. Simple baseline predictor
pfun <- function(s_tr, y_tr, s_new) {
  rep(mean(y_tr), nrow(s_new))
}

# 3. Execution triggering the issue
out <- scp_geostatistical(s_train, y_train, s_test, pfun, alpha = 0.1)
cov <- coverage_report(out, y_test)
print(cov)

# 4. Environment details
sessionInfo()
